Venezuela Lifts Temporary Oil Export Ban, Industry Operations Resume

Caracas – Oil and gas producers in Venezuela have resumed export operations following the government’s decision to lift a temporary ban on crude oil and refined product shipments. The measure, which was implemented three weeks ago amid concerns over revenue leakage and irregularities at key shipping terminals, had severely disrupted export schedules and strained storage capacity across the sector.

According to the Ministry of Petroleum, the embargo was imposed as a “preventive step to safeguard national interests and ensure regulatory compliance.” In a statement released on Tuesday, Petroleum Minister Ignacio Rodríguez announced that “the necessary corrective actions have been taken, and export operations are now authorized to continue under enhanced oversight.”

The embargo had halted the loading of tankers at major ports, including Puerto Miranda and Jose Terminal, affecting companies such as PetroAndina and Orinoco Energy. Several industry analysts estimate that daily crude exports fell by as much as 48% during the stoppage, with some 5 million barrels stockpiled.

“The suspension created significant logistical challenges, but we are working around the clock to clear the backlog and meet contractual obligations,” said Maria Guzmán, spokesperson for the National Oil Producers Association. She added that most facilities were able to maintain upstream operations at reduced rates, preventing major shutdowns.

Union leader Rafael Moreno noted, “Workers remained on site to ensure equipment integrity and safety. Now, with exports resuming, we expect a gradual normalization of activity and employment levels.”

Industry sources indicate that customs authorities have introduced new electronic monitoring systems to prevent future irregularities. Analysts project that export levels will return to pre-ban volumes by the end of the month.
